questions.question: What are wait(), notify(), and notifyAll() in Java?
questions.title: wait(), notify(), and notifyAll() in Java
questions.direct_answer: `wait()` makes the current thread **release the lock and wait** until notified. `notify()` wakes up **one** waiting thread. `notifyAll()` wakes up **all** waiting threads. All three must be called inside a **synchronized block** on the same object.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands inter-thread communication
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing these must be called inside synchronized — will throw IllegalMonitorStateException
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why wait() is in a while loop, not if, to guard against spurious wakeups

sections.title: How wait/notify Works
sections.content:
wait/notify is Java's mechanism for threads to **coordinate on a condition**:

1. Thread A calls `obj.wait()` inside `synchronized(obj)` — it **releases** the lock and enters WAITING
2. Thread B calls `obj.notify()` inside `synchronized(obj)` — one waiting thread is woken up
3. Woken thread re-acquires the lock and checks the condition again

Key rules:
- Must be in `synchronized` block on the same object — else `IllegalMonitorStateException`
- Use **while loop** (not if) to check the condition — guards against spurious wakeups
- `wait()` releases the lock; `sleep()` does NOT

sections.title: Producer-Consumer with wait/notify
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: wait(), notify(), and notifyAll() are on the Object class and they're the classic mechanism for inter-thread communication in Java. All three must be called inside a synchronized block on the same object — if you call wait() outside synchronized, you get an IllegalMonitorStateException. When wait() is called, the thread releases the lock and enters a WAITING state. When notify() is called, one waiting thread is woken up. That thread then tries to re-acquire the lock and continue. An important pattern: always check your condition in a while loop, not an if. If the condition changes again before the woken thread actually runs, it needs to loop back and wait again. This also guards against spurious wakeups.

questions.question: Why must wait() and notify() be called inside a synchronized block?
questions.title: wait() and notify() Inside synchronized Block
questions.direct_answer: Because wait/notify operate on the **object's monitor** — the intrinsic lock. Calling wait() releases the monitor; calling notify() signals waiting threads on the monitor. If you don't hold the monitor, the JVM has nothing to release or signal on, so it throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that calling wait() outside synchronized throws IllegalMonitorStateException

sections.title: Why synchronized is Required
sections.content:
Without the synchronized requirement, a **missed notification** race condition would occur:

1. Consumer checks: buffer is empty (true)
2. **Context switch to Producer**
3. Producer adds item and calls notify() — no one is waiting yet
4. **Context switch back to Consumer**
5. Consumer calls wait() — waits forever (missed the notification)

With synchronized:
1. Consumer holds the lock when checking buffer is empty
2. Producer cannot call notify() until consumer releases the lock (by calling wait())
3. wait() atomically releases the lock AND starts waiting
4. No notification can be missed

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: The synchronized requirement exists to prevent missed notifications. Imagine wait() and notify() didn't need synchronized. A consumer could check 'is buffer empty — yes', then get context switched out before calling wait(). The producer runs, adds an item, calls notify(), but nobody is waiting yet. Then the consumer runs and calls wait() — waiting forever, having missed the notification. The synchronized requirement prevents this by making the check-and-wait atomic. Inside synchronized, the consumer checks the condition and calls wait() in one uninterruptible step. The producer can't sneak in with notify() between the check and the wait.

questions.question: What is the difference between notify() and notifyAll()?
questions.title: notify() vs notifyAll() in Java
questions.direct_answer: `notify()` wakes up **one arbitrarily chosen** waiting thread. `notifyAll()` wakes up **all** waiting threads. `notifyAll()` is generally safer — if only one thread is waiting for a specific condition, using notify() might wake the wrong thread.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the subtle bug that notify() can cause when multiple types of waiters exist
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always using notify() thinking it's more efficient — it can cause lost wakeups
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the specific scenario where notify() causes a bug: multiple waiters with different conditions

sections.title: notify() vs notifyAll()
sections.content:
| Aspect | notify() | notifyAll() |
|---|---|---|
| Threads woken | One (random) | All waiting |
| Performance | Slightly better | More overhead |
| Safety | Can cause starvation | Safer |
| Use case | One type of waiter | Multiple waiter types |
| Risk | Wrong thread woken | All threads compete for lock |

sections.title: When notify() Causes Bugs
sections.content:
If threads wait for different conditions on the same object:
- Thread A waits for: buffer not empty
- Thread B waits for: buffer not full

If producer calls `notify()` and wakes Thread B (wrong type), Thread B checks 'buffer not full' — still true — goes back to wait. Nothing actually processes the item. Use `notifyAll()` to wake all threads and let each check their own condition.

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: notify() wakes one random waiting thread; notifyAll() wakes all of them. When should you use which? Use notifyAll() when there are multiple types of threads waiting on the same object for different conditions. If you use notify() in that case, you might wake a thread that's waiting for the wrong condition — it goes back to sleep and nothing happens. All woken threads will check their condition and the wrong ones will just wait again. notify() is safe when there's only one type of waiter and any one of them can proceed. In practice, when in doubt, use notifyAll() — it's safer, and the overhead of waking extra threads is usually acceptable.

questions.question: What is a spurious wakeup and how do you handle it?
questions.title: Spurious Wakeup in Java
questions.direct_answer: A **spurious wakeup** is when a waiting thread wakes up without being notified. This is allowed by the POSIX specification and can happen on any platform. The defense is to **always check the condition in a while loop** after waking up, not just an if statement.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of a subtle but important threading edge case
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using if instead of while — code works in most tests but fails in rare production scenarios
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the correct while-loop pattern and explain why the JVM spec allows spurious wakeups

sections.title: Handling Spurious Wakeups
Why Spurious Wakeups Exist
sections.content:
The POSIX standard for threads (which the JVM implements on Linux) allows wait() to return even without a corresponding signal. This happens at the OS level due to hardware signals or kernel implementation details. The Java spec explicitly acknowledges this and says: always recheck your condition after waking.

The `while` loop pattern:
1. Thread wakes up (spuriously or via notify)
2. Re-acquires the lock
3. Checks condition: if still not met → wait again
4. If met → proceed

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: A spurious wakeup is when a thread that called wait() wakes up even though nobody called notify() on it. This is permitted by the POSIX specification that the JVM builds on — it's a known low-level behavior. The Java documentation actually explicitly says to always check the condition in a while loop, not an if. So the pattern is while the condition isn't met, wait again. If the wakeup was spurious, the while loop catches it and the thread waits again. If the condition is now met, the loop exits and the thread proceeds. Using if instead of while is a subtle bug that works 99.9% of the time but can cause rare production issues.

speakable_v2.hook: Spurious wakeups are allowed by the Java spec — a thread can wake up from wait() without any notify() being called.

beats.text: A spurious wakeup is when a thread wakes up from wait() without any notify() or notifyAll() being called. This is explicitly permitted by the POSIX specification (which the JVM builds on) and acknowledged in the Java documentation. The defense is always checking the condition in a while loop.

On certain Linux kernel versions and hardware, OS-level signals can wake blocked threads. The JVM can't distinguish a spurious OS signal from a genuine notify(). Rather than adding expensive detection, the spec shifts responsibility to the developer: always recheck the condition after waking.

items: While loop: thread wakes, reacquires lock, checks condition — if still not met, waits again.
If statement (wrong): thread wakes, reacquires lock, skips condition check, proceeds with stale state.
Java docs explicitly say: 'wait should always be used in a loop'.

beats.text: sharp edge: Spurious wakeups are very rare — your code might pass all tests and work for months in production before one occurs. But when it does, using if instead of while means the thread processes a null item, divides by zero, or accesses invalid state. The while loop costs one extra condition check per genuine wakeup — a tiny price for correctness.

items: Using if for the wait condition check looks fine in all tests and almost all production runs — until it isn't.

questions.question: What class do wait() and notify() belong to and why?
questions.title: Why wait() and notify() Are on Object Class
questions.direct_answer: `wait()` and `notify()` are on the **Object class** because every Java object can serve as a **monitor (lock)**. Since synchronization can be done on any object, the wait/notify mechanism must be available on every object too.

interviewer_intent.testing: Conceptual understanding — why these methods are on Object, not Thread

interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the monitor/lock ownership requirement and why it naturally belongs to Object

sections.title: Why Object, Not Thread
sections.content:
In Java, every object has an intrinsic lock (monitor). The `synchronized` keyword acquires this lock. Since you can synchronize on any object (`synchronized(anyObject) {}`), the wait/notify mechanism needs to be tied to whatever object you're locking.

If wait/notify were on Thread:
- You'd have to know which thread to notify — but you usually don't
- You'd lose the connection to the shared data object

On Object:
- `buffer.wait()` — wait while holding buffer's lock, associated with buffer
- `buffer.notify()` — notify threads waiting on buffer's lock
- The object IS the shared resource AND the synchronization point

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: wait() and notify() are on Object because every Java object can be a lock. The synchronized keyword can be used with any object — synchronized(myList), synchronized(this), synchronized(someOtherObject). So the wait/notify mechanism needs to be available on every object too. The other reason: wait and notify are about coordinating around a shared resource. If you're waiting on a buffer to have items, it makes semantic sense to call buffer.wait() and buffer.notify() — the buffer IS the synchronization point. If these were on Thread, you'd need to track which threads to notify, which is much harder and doesn't map naturally to the shared data you're coordinating around.

beats.text: Every Java object has an intrinsic lock (monitor). The synchronized keyword can be used on any object. Since wait() and notify() operate on the object's monitor — releasing it, waiting on it — they have to be methods on Object so they're available on every possible lock object.

If wait/notify were on Thread, you'd need to know which specific thread to wake — that's hard and doesn't model the problem well. The model is: threads coordinate around a shared resource (the object). It's the resource that says 'I'm ready' via notify(), not the thread.

items: buffer.wait(): wait while holding buffer's lock, because buffer is the shared resource.
buffer.notify(): signal threads waiting on buffer, because buffer is what changed.
The object IS the synchronization point — coordination lives on the resource, not the thread.

beats.text: non-obvious: You can call wait() on any object — including a String literal, though you really shouldn't. Synchronizing on a String literal is a bug because the same literal string is shared across the entire JVM. Other unrelated code using the same string could accidentally interfere with your lock.

items: Never synchronize or wait on String literals or boxed primitives — they're shared across the JVM.
Use a private dedicated lock object for maximum safety: private final Object lock = new Object();

speakable_v2.cap: wait/notify belongs to Object because synchronization belongs to objects — any object can be a condition variable in Java.

questions.question: How is BlockingQueue a better alternative to manual wait/notify?
questions.title: BlockingQueue vs Manual wait/notify
questions.direct_answer: **BlockingQueue** encapsulates the wait/notify logic for producer-consumer scenarios. `put()` blocks if full; `take()` blocks if empty — all synchronization is handled internally. This eliminates error-prone manual wait/notify code and spurious wakeup handling.

sections.title: BlockingQueue Producer-Consumer
Manual wait/notify vs BlockingQueue
sections.content:
| Aspect | Manual wait/notify | BlockingQueue |
|---|---|---|
| Code complexity | High (easy to get wrong) | Low |
| Spurious wakeup | Must handle manually | Handled internally |
| Missed notifications | Risk if not careful | No risk |
| Type safety | Generic code | Typed |
| Production use | Rarely needed | Preferred |

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: BlockingQueue is a much better choice for producer-consumer scenarios than manual wait/notify. It handles all the synchronization internally — put() blocks if the queue is full, take() blocks if it's empty. You don't write any synchronized blocks, don't worry about spurious wakeups, and don't risk missed notifications. The two common implementations are ArrayBlockingQueue with a fixed capacity and LinkedBlockingQueue which can optionally be unbounded. In practice, whenever I need producer-consumer coordination, I reach for BlockingQueue. Manual wait/notify is something you understand conceptually — and interviewers test you on it — but in production code, you'd use the higher-level abstraction.
